entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer as an evolving system, combining experimental, computational and AI/ML approaches. A central aim is to quantify and forecast tumour evolution, including very early evolution in precancer settings such as Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia. The lab also links genotype to phenotype in malignancy using multiomic profiling, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and organoid and computational models. A further goal is building reliable biomarkers to guide diagnosis, early detection and treatment decisions.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on cancer genomics, computational/ML methods and single-cell and spatial omics in cancer, with less emphasis on structural variants or bulk WGS/transcriptome pipelines; a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI/ML models for in silico functional genomics. These include interpretable models of DNA and RNA regulation, plus large language and foundation models for chemistry and genomics. In cancer biology, it studies how tumour cells evolve and interact with their environment, with a focus on metastatic progression. Its work includes orphan non-coding RNAs (oncRNAs) that promote metastasis, and tRNA-derived fragments (tiRNAs) that suppress breast cancer metastasis. It also studies post-transcriptional regulatory programs in disease, and applies the same approach to neurodegenerative diseases.

fit.reason: The lab's ML for genomics and its cancer transcriptome and non-coding RNA work overlap with the student's interests. Its focus is metastasis and RNA regulation, not tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Van Loo Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses "molecular archeology of cancer" approaches to reconstruct how tumours evolve. It looks at evolutionary history, subclonal structure, metastatic spread and the emergence of therapy resistance. The work relies on computational analysis of large-scale cancer genomics data, including whole-genome sequencing, copy number and clonal evolution inference. It combines pan-cancer cohort studies with focused studies of individual tumour types.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with tumour WGS, somatic mutation and copy-number analysis, and computational methods for cancer genomics. Single-cell and spatial work is not evident from the pages I read, and a US visa may be needed.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the causes of cancer by analysing patterns of somatic mutation, known as mutational signatures, in tumour and normal-tissue genomes. A major strand is Mutographs, a consortium collecting about 5,000 cancer samples from more than 25 countries to identify the exposures behind these signatures. The lab also maintains the SigProfiler suite of machine-learning tools for next-generation sequencing data. Further work covers the mutational landscape of precancerous lesions (2,561 samples from 37 lesion types), duplex sequencing of normal tissues, and the Cancer Grand Challenges CAUSE project on DNA adducts.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation analysis, whole-genome cancer sequencing, structural/copy-number signatures and ML methods; little single-cell or spatial omics and no transcriptome focus, and the lab is in the US so a visa would be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer genomes through two linked steps. Characterization catalogues somatic and germline events and their causes by comparing tumour and normal samples. Interpretation analyses patient cohorts to find cancer-driving genes, pathways and molecular subtypes, and to relate them to clinical parameters and treatment outcomes. It builds computational tools and pipelines for large national and international cancer genome projects (for example TCGA and the Broad's genome and proteogenomics data analysis centres). These cover somatic mutation calling, resistance mechanisms and germline cancer risk.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's cancer genomics, tumour WGS/somatic mutation analysis and computational methods interests, though I did not verify specific structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work. The US location may require a visa.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI-driven, mechanistic models of cancer and neurodegenerative disease. The aim is to turn patient data into precision diagnosis and treatment. It maps genetic and molecular networks, such as the U2OS subcellular cell map and the Cancer Cell Map Initiative, and uses them to predict how genotype affects outcomes. It develops 'visible' (interpretable) machine learning for predictive oncology, including a recent foundation model that predicts therapeutic response from cancer genotype. Other work covers network biomarkers, the link between somatic mutation and epigenetic aging, and software such as Cytoscape, NDEx and iQuery.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's cancer genomics, somatic mutation and ML-for-genomics interests, but it centres on network and interpretable-ML models rather than WGS/transcriptome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and it would likely require a US visa.

entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab studies how evolution can be learned from data and then used for design. One theme is learning from nature: how the immune system balances short-term protection with long-term adaptability, with the aim of designing more robust therapeutics. A second theme is accelerating evolution by using machine learning to learn evolutionary rules from sequence data. A third theme is safe biological AI, meaning generative models that let researchers quickly counter harmful biology. Most of the work is machine learning on biological sequences.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops single-cell technologies and computational methods to learn the molecular and environmental rules behind cell fate decisions in development, regeneration and disease. Model systems include zebrafish, intestinal organoids, human airway epithelium, Ciona and hematopoietic systems. Computational work covers lineage-resolved inference, noise quantification, and statistical and predictive models of tissue behaviour.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies statistical and computational methods that combine large-scale human genetics (GWAS and sequencing) with functional genomics and systems biology. The aim is to identify causal genes, regulatory variants and cell types in common eye diseases, mainly primary open-angle glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy. Methods include eQTL integration (the PI is a GTEx core team member), single-cell RNA-seq and whole-genome sequencing from human eye tissues, and a multi-lab human eye cell atlas. Newer work uses perturbational expression profiles to find drug-repurposing opportunities. The lab studies germline genetic risk in a non-cancer disease context and does no cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab's computational methods and single-cell genomics overlap with the student's interests, but the lab studies germline GWAS and eye disease, not tumour sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutation or cancer, and it is in the US, so a visa may be needed.

Current topics include large language models for biological sequences, machine learning for structural biology (protein structure, diffusion models, antibody design), and uncertainty estimation and calibration. It also works on privacy-preserving genomic analytics and algorithmic (compressive) genomics. Single-cell work includes graph representation learning, regulatory genomics and causal inference for single-cell data. Past work covers network biology and population genetics.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interest in computational and ML methods and, partly, single-cell omics, but it centres on protein and structure ML, with no focus on cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variants; a US move would also need a visa.

entries.name: Patel Lab
entries.focus: The group builds computational and AI tools that analyse genetics and the environment together to understand inter-individual differences in health. It integrates proteomic, regulomic and exposomic data (including the microbiome) with electronic medical records. It also uses real-world signals such as wearables, insurance claims and satellite data. The group co-leads NEXUS, the Network for Exposomics in the United States, which builds infrastructure for lifelong environmental exposure data. Its machine-learning work projects individual health trajectories for conditions such as Alzheimer's, cancer and diabetes. It also develops meta-science methods, such as the 'vibration of effects', to make big-data findings more robust.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and machine-learning methods, but its focus is exposomics and epidemiology. It does not work on tumour WGS or transcriptome sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutation analysis, or single-cell or spatial cancer omics.

entries.name: Smillie Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses combined computational and experimental systems approaches to study host-microbiome interactions in the gut. One area is building cell atlases of the human colon and enteric nervous system, and using spatial transcriptomics to see how microbes affect human cell development and function. A second area is microbiome evolution during disease, including horizontal gene transfer, bacterial strain tracking and microbial adaptation in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). A third area is computational methods for spatial and single-cell transcriptomics, including cell-cell interaction inference and linking human-genetics risk loci to cells and pathways. The work is not cancer-focused.

fit.reason: The lab's single-cell, spatial omics and computational methods work overlaps with the student's interests, but its focus is the gut microbiome and IBD rather than cancer, tumour sequencing or structural variants. The student would also likely need a US visa.

entries.name: Coley Group
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning and computational tools for chemistry and drug discovery. Main topics are computer-aided synthesis planning and retrosynthesis, reaction outcome and mechanism prediction, and generative models for small-molecule and 3D structure-based drug design. A second thread is structure elucidation, in which ML turns tandem mass spectrometry data into molecular structures (computational metabolomics). A third thread closes the loop with automated experimentation, using high-throughput and autonomous labs, LLM agents and process-aware optimization. The work is almost entirely chemistry and small-molecule oriented, with no genomics focus.

entries.name: Huttenhower Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for studying microbial communities, especially the human microbiome. This includes functional profiling of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes and taxonomic and strain-level profiling. It also covers multi-omics integration and statistical association methods for microbiome epidemiology. The lab applies these methods to cohort studies of IBD (the HMP2/IBDMDB project), diet, and colorectal cancer. It also builds widely used software tools, including the bioBakery suite (MetaPhlAn, HUMAnN) and MaAsLin. It runs the Harvard Chan Microbiome Analysis Core. The work is mostly microbial and host-microbiome, with only a modest overlap with human tumour genomics.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and statistical methods for genomics and has some microbiome-cancer epidemiology, but it does not work on tumour WGS, structural variants, somatic mutations or single-cell/spatial cancer omics. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Korsunsky Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds computational methods and software for genomic data with complex study designs. Its best-known tool is Harmony, which integrates single-cell data across donors and studies. A second line of work analyzes spatially resolved gene and protein expression with collaborators, to reconstruct pathological tissue structures in inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease. The lab also compares inflammatory cell phenotypes across diseases to separate tissue-specific from shared states. Current members work on spatial transcriptomics (e.g. Xenium) and Bayesian machine learning.

entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics and genomics to find genes and variants that influence common diseases and traits, especially height, obesity, and the timing of puberty. The lab also develops computational methods for extracting biology from genetic data.

entries.name: Desai Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines theory and high-throughput experiments to study evolutionary dynamics and population genetics. Experimental work uses budding yeast (thousands of lines evolved in parallel, including 10,000+ generation experiments) and the E. coli long-term evolution experiment, with molecular barcoding to track lineages. A major theme is high-dimensional genotype-phenotype maps and epistasis, using theory, quantitative genetics trait mapping in yeast, and machine learning for trait prediction and protein sequence-function landscapes. A growing branch covers pathogen–immune coevolution, including viral antigen evolution, antibody and B-cell receptor affinity maturation in the germinal center, and microbe-immune interactions.

fit.reason: Their computational and machine-learning methods for genomics and quantitative genetics are loosely relevant, but the lab studies microbial and viral evolution and immune coevolution, not cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial cancer omics.

entries.focus: The lab works on engineering biology for sustainability, including genetic tools for the industrial-scale-capable bacterium Xanthobacter to make commodities from low-cost substrates. entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetics of diabetes, covering rare through common variation, to find new diabetes genes, disease subtypes and mechanisms. A signature approach is partitioned polygenic scores and clustering of type 2 diabetes loci. These group genetic risk by biological pathway, and the lab uses them to define molecular subtypes of type 2 diabetes across ancestries. The team analyses large genomic and clinical datasets (UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, All of Us, the Type 2 Diabetes Knowledge Portal) and links genetics to electronic health records. It leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT atypical diabetes study and works with the Florez Lab. Members also see patients in the MGH Diabetes Genetics Clinic, and some projects cover pharmacogenomics and obesity.

fit.reason: The lab does computational statistical genetics (GWAS, polygenic scores, clustering) in diabetes, so it overlaps only with the student's interest in computational genomics methods and not with cancer genomics, tumour WGS or RNA-seq, structural or somatic variants, or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Sabeti Lab
entries.focus: The lab tracks how outbreaks emerge, spread and evolve using pathogen genomic sequencing, with work on Ebola, Lassa, Zika, mumps and SARS-CoV-2 and programs in Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Senegal. It develops tools for pandemic preemption, including Cas13/CRISPR-based diagnostics, machine-learning-optimized assay design, unbiased deep sequencing and hybrid capture for virus discovery. It studies viral evolution and virus-host interactions, including single-cell profiling of Ebola and other BL-4 pathogens and massively parallel mapping of viral peptides presented to the immune system. A fourth line covers human genetic variation, using massively parallel reporter assays for non-coding variants, directed evolution of viral capsids, and demographic simulation plus machine learning to detect selection.

fit.reason: The lab has strong computational genomics, machine learning and some single-cell methods, but its work is on pathogens and human population genetics rather than cancer genomics, structural variants or somatic mutation, and a move to the US would likely need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab asks how a biological system's history shapes its future. It works in three steps: make histories observable, infer how history determines fate with mathematical models, and then perturb systems to test the inferred rules. Current projects include DNA-based lineage and signaling recording, barcoding with in situ readout alongside transcriptomes, live imaging of cell families in mammalian 'mother machines', and human gastruloid and synthetic-embryo models. Other projects reconstruct the origins and clonal expansion of blood cancers using population genetics and stochastic models, develop single-cell RNA-seq for bacteria, and study experimental HIV and viral evolution.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops tools to tune gene regulation in small, measured steps rather than all-or-nothing. It uses these tools to study how gene regulation works and how it fails in disease. Its main focus is transcription factor (TF) dosage. Changes of 50% or less in TF levels can cause rare disorders or common trait variation. The lab perturbs TF dosage in human pluripotent stem cells and their derivatives, including neural crest cells, which form the craniofacial skeleton and the enteric nervous system. It combines functional genomics, such as multi-omic profiling and enhancer mapping, with computational and predictive modelling. The aim is to find the regulatory elements, genes and cell states most sensitive to dosage, and so most likely to drive disease.

entries.name: Ovchinnikov Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how proteins evolve, at scales from the molecular to the environmental. It aims for a unified model of protein evolution that combines phylogenetic inference, protein structure prediction and design, and deep learning. Recent work includes CIRPIN, a graph neural network that learns structure representations invariant to circular permutation and is used to find remote homologs. It also includes MSA Pairformer, a compact MSA-based protein language model of coevolution between interacting proteins (published in Cell). The lab also applies generative protein design to applied problems, for example binders against citrus-greening disease.

fit.reason: The lab works on protein evolution, structure and design with deep learning, with no cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is the general use of ML for biology, and a US visa may also be needed.

entries.name: Sunyaev Lab
entries.focus: The Sunyaev Lab is a computational genomics group that studies human genetic variation from evolutionary, functional and medical angles. Its main topics are the biology and evolution of mutation (mutation rate maps, mutagenesis mechanisms, DNA repair), population genetics of deleterious alleles and negative selection, and the allelic architecture of complex traits. The lab develops statistical and machine-learning methods for sequencing studies and for predicting the effects of coding variants (PolyPhen-2, DeMAG for Mendelian disease genes). It also has projects in cancer genomics, including modelling tumour progression, and in applied human genetics such as rare-variant analysis in neurodegeneration.

entries.name: Raychaudhuri Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics, genomics and immunology to work out the basis of rheumatoid arthritis and other immune-mediated diseases. It builds statistical and computational methods to pinpoint causal genetic variants and to interpret human genetic data using functional information. It runs human genetics and functional genomics programs in tuberculosis, type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. It also uses single-cell genomics to study tissue inflammation, mainly in CD4+ T cells and fibroblasts. The lab is part of the IGVF, ITN and AMP AIM consortia.

fit.reason: The lab is strong on computational methods and single-cell omics, which overlap with the student's methods interests. Its focus is germline GWAS and autoimmune disease rather than cancer, tumour WGS/RNA-seq or somatic structural variants, so the topical overlap is small.

entries.focus: The lab studies the genomics of childhood brain tumours (especially medulloblastoma and pediatric low-grade glioma) and leukaemias, with an emphasis on their developmental origins and driver mechanisms. The lab works closely with wet-lab and clinical collaborators (for example, a joint postdoc posting with the Stegmaier Lab). It has also advertised postdoc openings in computational genomics and in biostatistics/machine learning.

entries.name: Zhou Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds statistical methods for finding genetic risk factors for disease in large biobanks. Tools include SAIGE, SAIGE-GENE(+) and GATE, which handle phenome-wide association scans, rare-variant tests and time-to-event analyses. Wei Zhou co-leads the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative (GBMI), which combines FinnGen, HUNT, UK Biobank, All of Us and other biobanks. The lab also studies disease onset and progression using long-term health records. A newer direction links genetic associations to biological mechanism through multi-omics, currently scalable single-cell eQTL mapping.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and statistical methods for genomics, and its single-cell eQTL work is a minor overlap. Its focus is germline population genetics in biobanks, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS/RNA-seq or somatic structural variants, so the overlap is small.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods for large-scale genetic and genomic data. Its work covers whole-genome sequencing association tests for rare and noncoding variants (STAAR), functional annotation of variants (FAVOR), polygenic risk prediction, and heritability estimation. It also works on causal inference and mediation analysis, integrating genetic, clinical and plasma protein data, and predicting gene expression from genotype. More recent work applies manifold learning, optimal transport and generative modelling to single-cell and spatial multiomic data, including the IGVF consortium. The lab's emphasis is on population-scale biobank and human-genetics statistics. Tumour genomics is not a stated focus on the pages I checked.

entries.name: Reshef Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies machine learning and statistical methods to quantitatively characterize autoimmunity. A core theme is comparing immune state across samples from high-dimensional molecular data, especially single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Published examples include co-varying neighbourhood analysis (CNA) to find cell populations associated with phenotypes (Nature Biotechnology 2021) and case-control analysis methods for spatial molecular data (Nature Methods 2026). Earlier work includes statistical genetics, such as the directional effects of transcription factor binding on polygenic disease risk (Nature Genetics 2018). The work is methods-driven and applied to immune-mediated disease, not cancer.

fit.reason: The lab's computational and ML methods for single-cell and spatial omics match the student's methods interests, but its focus is autoimmunity, not cancer, and it has no tumour WGS or structural-variant work.

Collaborations increasingly address the genomics of human disease, including Alzheimer's dementia, cancer and Mendelian musculoskeletal disorders.

entries.name: Rothenberg Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (gene regulatory network modelling; T-cell development)
entries.focus: The lab studies how multipotent blood progenitors commit to the T-cell lineage in the thymus. They treat this as a problem in gene regulatory network (GRN) logic. They examine how transcription factors such as Bcl11b, Lmo2, Hhex and others change in dosage and timing to control lineage choice and developmental pace. Current projects include age-related shifts in thymocyte potential toward innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and innate-like γδ T cells. Another project uses quantitative proteomics to map protein-level regulation. Methods combine mouse and in vitro T-cell differentiation systems, genomic and epigenomic profiling, perturbation experiments, and computational GRN modelling.

fit.reason: The lab is strong in computational and genomic GRN analysis, but it studies normal T-cell development rather than cancer genomics, tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, so the overlap is limited to general genomics methods.

entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Computation and Neural Systems / Bioengineering (molecular programming)
entries.focus: The group takes a synthetic approach to molecular programming. They build DNA- and RNA-based systems to find out what can be engineered with nucleic acids. Topics include algorithmic DNA self-assembly (tile assembly and DNA origami), in vitro biochemical circuits based on strand displacement, and chemical reaction networks. They also study DNA and RNA folding, fault-tolerant molecular computing, molecular self-replication, and the fundamental limits of computation in these systems. Current members also work on molecular motors, DNA condensates and liquid-liquid phase separation, and pattern formation in synthetic biology.

fit.reason: The lab does DNA nanotechnology and molecular computation, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work, so it overlaps almost nothing with the student's interests.

entries.focus: The lab works on three areas: cytoskeletal active matter, machine learning, and single-cell biology. One student works on tumour heterogeneity and cell-cell communication.

entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (experimental plus computational genomics)
entries.focus: The lab studies how non-coding RNAs shape nuclear structure and gene expression. A major model is the lncRNA Xist and X-chromosome inactivation. The lab also studies nuclear compartments such as nuclear speckles and their link to splicing efficiency, and RNA-mediated neurodegeneration (the C9ORF72 repeat expansion in ALS). It builds its own multiplexed genomics tools, including SPRITE (3D genome contacts among DNA, RNA and protein), CLAP and SPIDR (RNA-protein interaction mapping) and ChIP-DIP (protein-DNA mapping). It combines these experimental methods with computational analysis, and its newer work includes single-cell functional genomics and CRISPRi screens.

fit.reason: The lab combines genomics method development with computation and some single-cell work, but it focuses on basic RNA and nuclear biology, with no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant or somatic mutation work. A US visa may also be needed.

entries.focus: The lab builds hardware, molecular and software tools to study genome regulation in single cells and single molecules. The work is mostly technology development and basic biology, not cancer genomics.

entries.focus: The group studies somatic mutations in normal human cells and uses them as inherent barcodes for development and the origins of cancer. entries.focus: The group uses evolutionary biology to understand and predict how individual cancers develop, metastasise and become drug resistant. Its work centres on clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and melanoma. The team mixes cancer geneticists, computational biologists and clinician scientists, and is linked to the TRACERx Renal study.

entries.name: Page Lab
entries.focus: The Page lab studies how males and females differ genetically, both in and outside the reproductive tract, and how those differences affect biology and medicine. Its work spans comparative, evolutionary, developmental and clinical analyses. It sequenced the sex chromosomes of eight mammals and chickens. That work found Y-linked genes that are active throughout the body and regulate chromatin, transcription, translation and protein stability. Current questions include how sex chromosome makeup (X and Y dosage) shapes sex differences in gene expression and sex biases in disease. The lab also develops methods for highly accurate sequencing of complex, repetitive genomic regions. It uses mouse models to study germ cell development, which bears on infertility and germ cell cancers.

fit.reason: The lab has strong computational genomics and sequencing methods, and it touches germ cell cancers, but its main focus is sex-chromosome biology and not tumour WGS, structural variants, somatic mutations or single-cell/spatial cancer omics. A US visa would also likely be needed.

entries.name: Mirny Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the 3D organization of the genome and how it is established, using polymer physics and biophysical modelling. A central topic is loop extrusion by cohesin and condensin SMC complexes, and how it shapes chromatin folding, enhancer-promoter communication and sister chromatid organization. Related work covers epigenetic memory through mitosis and cell fate, and the nuclear mechanics and organization of chromatin. Methods are mainly polymer simulations, Hi-C and other chromosome-conformation data analysis, Bayesian inference and some machine learning. The lab has also done cancer-evolution work, including past students who went on to cancer genomics, but this is not its main current focus.

fit.reason: The lab is computational and uses Hi-C and some single-cell data, but it is focused on chromatin biophysics rather than cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutations, so overlap is limited to general computational-methods skills.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works on improving molecular dynamics force fields, which describe how atoms interact. Its main targets are disordered proteins and protein aggregation. One approach trains fast molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, using quantum mechanics and experimental data, to build a reproducible universal force field for biologically relevant molecules. A second approach develops machine learning interatomic potentials that are fast enough for biomolecular simulation, using simpler models and GPU programming. The long-term aim is to simulate enzyme reactions. Related work covers protein design with molecular simulation, free energy methods and protein folding.

fit.reason: The group does physics-based biomolecular simulation and ML force fields, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is general ML methods development.

entries.name: Scheres Group (cryo-EM computational methods, RELION)
entries.focus: The group develops image-processing methods for atomic-resolution structure determination by cryo-EM and cryo-ET. These are implemented in the open-source software RELION. They use the methods to solve structures of amyloid filaments extracted from the brains of people with neurodegenerative disease, in collaboration with Michel Goedert's group. Their work shows that one protein can adopt many amyloid folds; for example, tau forms filaments in more than 20 diseases, and different folds characterise different diseases. Current work includes in vitro assembly of amyloids that replicate brain-derived folds, tau and alpha-synuclein aggregation, and machine-learning methods for cryo-ET and protein design.

Several members work on single-cell and spatial transcriptomics methods, jointly with the Satija and Azizi labs.

entries.name: Skinnider Lab
entries.department_hint: Ludwig Princeton Branch / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods, built on AI and machine learning, to identify known and unknown small molecules from mass spectrometry data. It uses generative models for small-molecule structure elucidation and metabolite discovery. It combines these with biochemical experiments to map the mammalian metabolome and link metabolites to disease, including cancer. Related work with Martin Wühr applies machine learning to proteomics, specifically measuring absolute protein concentrations. The PI's earlier work covered computational proteomics and metabolomics, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics in spinal cord injury, and natural product discovery.

fit.reason: The lab's strengths are ML and computational methods, with some link to cancer, but it works on mass-spectrometry metabolomics, not tumour WGS/transcriptome, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics in cancer, and a US move would likely need a visa.

entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The group develops algorithms and machine learning methods for computational molecular biology. Main topics are predicting protein interactions, especially those mediated by short linear motifs and peptide-recognition domains, and predicting protein function. They also predict how missense and other mutations affect protein function and disease, and analyze biological networks. The work sits at the interface of computer science and molecular biology and is mostly computational, with experimental collaborations (for example, co-advised students with Wingreen and Donia).

entries.department_hint: Molecular Biology / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The lab uses theory and computational modeling to study how intracellular networks work in bacteria and other microorganisms. It also studies microbial communities, including how species interact and how communities are structured. A related line of work looks at the physics of biomolecular organization inside cells. The lab also collaborates on experimental methods, such as the single-cell bacterial RNA-seq method M3-seq. Specific methods were not verified on the lab's own pages.

fit.reason: The lab works on bacterial and microbial systems modeling, with only a loose link to the student's computational and single-cell interests; it has no cancer genomics, structural variant or tumour sequencing work.

entries.name: Laboratory of Bioinformatics and Functional Genomics
entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and machine-learning methods for functional genomics. It integrates large-scale experimental datasets to infer gene function and to build tissue- and cell-type-specific gene and protein interaction networks. It also develops deep-learning models of how genomic sequence and noncoding variation affect regulation and disease. Its work includes human genetics and precision-health applications, such as a 2025 study of biologically distinct autism subtypes. The Princeton pages I fetched give only a brief research description, so this summary partly relies on the lab's onboarding page and my own prior knowledge of the group's work.

fit.reason: The lab's strong computational and machine-learning methods for genomics match one of the student's interests, but I found no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural-variant, or single-cell/spatial focus on the pages I checked, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods to design and analyze high-throughput functional genomic assays and perturbations. Its emphasis is on multi-modal single-cell, spatial and genome-editing technologies. It uses statistics, machine learning and efficient algorithms to integrate multi-dimensional data. The biological applications are regulatory genomics and cell-cell interactions in vivo, mainly in immunology and cancer.

entries.name: Torkamani Lab (Genome Informatics, Translational Institute)
entries.focus: The lab uses genomic and informatic technologies to find the genetic causes and mechanisms of human disease. Its main areas are human genome interpretation and discovery of novel rare diseases. It also builds machine- and deep-learning models to predict common-disease risk, including polygenic risk scores for conditions such as coronary artery disease (a 2025 Scripps study). A further area is genetically informed digital communication of disease risk, as in the MyGeneRank app. The work is mostly germline and population-scale, not tumour-focused.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and machine-learning methods for genomics, but its work is germline, rare-disease and risk-prediction, with little on cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptome, somatic structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.focus: The Su Lab builds and applies bioinformatics tools and infrastructure for biomedical discovery, with an emphasis on open source, open data and open science. A recurring theme is crowdsourcing and community curation for genetics and genomics. The lab also uses bioinformatics to generate testable biomedical hypotheses. The pages I read describe this work as knowledge-graph, data-integration and text-mining infrastructure, not tumour sequencing or variant calling.

fit.reason: The lab's work is on knowledge bases, annotation tools and crowdsourcing. It has little direct overlap with tumour WGS/transcriptome analysis, structural variants or single-cell/spatial cancer omics, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Kennedy Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how biological systems combine external cues with internal state to guide action. Questions range from single neurons to social groups, with an emphasis on fear, survival and social behaviours. Methods are mathematical modelling and model-informed data analysis, drawing on dynamical systems, control theory, reinforcement learning and machine learning. Current projects include spiking-network dynamics, computational tools for quantifying animal behaviour across timescales, and neuromodulation and population coding. The lab also stresses open science and community resources.

fit.reason: The lab does theoretical and computational neuroscience of behaviour and neural circuits. It has no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work. The only overlap is generic machine-learning methods.

entries.name: Hogenesch Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies circadian biology and temporal genomics, meaning how the body clock shapes gene expression and physiology. It also builds public data resources and works on circadian medicine, such as how clock disruption drives metabolic disease risk and biomarker discovery. It combines experimental biology (functional models of rare genetic disease, patient-derived disease models) with computational methods, including the CYCLOPS algorithm for reconstructing circadian time from unordered samples. The team mixes experimental biologists, computational scientists and clinician-scientists, with a focus on human genetics and sleep. I did not find cancer work on the lab pages I read.

fit.reason: The lab's computational circadian-genomics and time-series expression methods overlap slightly with the student's interest in computational and machine-learning genomics, but there is no evident cancer genomics, structural variant or single-cell/spatial focus, and a US move would likely need a visa.

Work combines large international sequencing collaborations with evolutionary and computational analysis.

entries.name: Mravic Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses protein design and integrative computational approaches to study how proteins work, mainly inside cell membranes. One area is the design of small synthetic membrane proteins as simple model systems for basic biophysics questions. A second area is the de novo design and high-throughput engineering of chemical biology tools that target the lipid-embedded regions of membrane proteins, including GPCRs. A third area is molecular modeling and dynamics simulation that combines diverse experimental data. A recent postdoc/staff-scientist posting also mentions cryo-EM, AI-driven protein and peptide design, and high-throughput screening.

fit.reason: The lab works on membrane protein design and biophysics, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant, or single-cell/spatial omics work; the only overlap is general computational and ML methods.

entries.name: Ken Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how RNA structural dynamics govern RNA-protein binding and function. This is done with computational and experimental methods, both in vitro and in cells. Current work centres on viral RNAs, especially quantitative modelling of how the HIV Gag polyprotein binds and oligomerizes on the HIV 5'-leader RNA to start genome packaging. A second theme is dynamics-based RNA drug targeting, which seeks rare, low-populated RNA conformations that small molecules could target. Methods include high-throughput mutational analysis of thousands of RNA variants, NMR, molecular dynamics, RNA structure prediction, and virtual screening with AutoDock.

fit.reason: The lab does RNA structural biology and antiviral drug discovery, with essentially no overlap with cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only link is a general computational/high-throughput flavour.

entries.name: Alsentzer Lab
entries.focus: The lab applies machine learning and natural language processing to support clinical decision-making and expand access to high-quality healthcare. One theme is integrating domain knowledge, such as biomedical knowledge graphs and unstructured clinical text, into models for generalizable decision support. A second is learning with limited annotated clinical data, using self-supervised learning and foundation models. A third is responsible ML: building and evaluating systems for equity, transparency and patient safety, with human-in-the-loop approaches. Recent work includes evaluating LLMs on real-world clinical text, monitoring deployed AI systems, and assessing AI-generated discharge summaries. Student projects also cover rare-disease diagnosis and reasoning over longitudinal clinical records alongside patient molecular data.

fit.reason: The lab does clinical ML and NLP on EHR text and has little work on cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell omics; only the general ML-methods interest and Jordan Cahoon's linking of clinical records to molecular data overlap, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of bioimaging, spatial proteomics and AI. Its goal is to define the spatiotemporal organization of the human proteome at the cellular and subcellular level. It maintains the Subcellular Atlas of the Human Protein Atlas (HPA), together with a Stockholm group. Methods include immunofluorescence microscopy, multiplexed imaging, mass-spectrometry proteomics and Deep Visual Proteomics. On the computational side, members build deep learning, self-supervised, diffusion and foundation models of protein localization and cell state, aiming at integrated models and 'digital twins' of human cells. Disease applications include primary cilia, cell migration and metastasis markers, and early cancer risk factors.

fit.reason: The lab's strengths are ML and spatial protein imaging, which loosely overlap with the student's interest in computational methods and spatial omics. It does essentially no cancer genomics, WGS/transcriptome sequencing or structural variant work, and the role would be in the US and need a visa.

The focus is germline and population genetics rather than tumour sequencing.

entries.name: Gevaert Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods for biomedical decision support, centred on 'biomedical data fusion'. This means integrating molecular (omics), cellular (pathology) and tissue-level (medical imaging) data. Its listed research areas are multi-omics data fusion, quantitative imaging (radiogenomics), computational pathology, computational epigenomics, and network modelling for drug discovery. Earlier work included Bayesian and kernel methods for breast and ovarian cancer, and algorithms that identify driver genes from multi-omics data. Current members work on deep learning for histology and genomics in brain cancer, digital pathology, and imaging-based prediction.

fit.reason: Strong overlap in cancer ML and multi-omics integration, but the lab emphasises imaging and pathology rather than WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Bioinformatics Group (UCL Computer Science)
entries.focus: The group develops machine learning and deep learning methods for protein bioinformatics. Its work covers protein structure prediction, protein function prediction and protein-protein interaction prediction. It also covers protein disorder, transmembrane protein analysis and de novo protein design. It is known for tools such as PSIPRED, GenTHREADER, MEMSAT and DISOPRED. Current work includes protein language models and representation learning on structural and learned embeddings. The group does not work on cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The group's machine-learning-for-biology methods loosely overlap with the student's interest in computational methods and ML for genomics. It is protein-focused, with no cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Hellenthal Group (statistical genetics, human population history)
entries.department_hint: Genetics, Evolution and Environment / UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The group develops statistical methods, including Bayesian approaches, for genome-wide genetic data. They use them to reconstruct human demographic history: population structure, admixture, migration and selection. Past projects include fine-scale genetic structure of the UK (People of the British Isles) and population movements in Ethiopia. Current members work on adaptation after the Anglo-Saxon migration using ancient DNA, ancestry in worldwide populations and adaptation to new environments, and early-embryo methylation marks that may affect long-term health.

fit.reason: The lab works on population-genetic and demographic inference in germline data, with no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant, somatic mutation or single-cell work. The only overlap is general statistical/computational genomics methods.

entries.name: MANIFOLD lab (machine learning, AI and neuroimaging for longevity and dementia)
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning and deep learning tools that turn brain MRI into clinically useful measures of brain ageing and neurodegeneration. Its signature topic is 'brain-age', where a model predicts age from neuroimaging and the gap from chronological age is used as an ageing biomarker. It also builds neuroanatomical normative models. It applies these to Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia and other neurological and psychiatric conditions. Large cohorts such as UK Biobank are used to link imaging markers to biomedical, lifestyle and cognitive factors.

fit.reason: The lab works on MRI-based brain ageing and dementia ML, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work. The only overlap is generic ML methodology.

entries.name: Bähler Lab (functional genomics, wet/dry)
entries.department_hint: Institute of Healthy Ageing / Genetics, Evolution and Environment
entries.focus: The lab studies the roles of conserved but uncharacterized genes in cellular quiescence, proliferation and ageing. The main models are fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe) and the African turquoise killifish. They combine wet-lab and computational functional genomics. This includes genome-wide screens, transcriptomics and other omics, metabolic and genomic regulation analyses, and natural variation in yeast. The lab also works with PomBase, the fission yeast community database, which has a biocurator in the group. A recent Wellcome Discovery Award funds the work on unknown genes.

entries.name: Computational Cancer Biology Group
entries.department_hint: Genetics, Evolution and Environment / UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The lab uses cancer as a model to study somatic evolution. One line of work asks how mutational processes drive cellular plasticity and adaptation to stress. The other asks how tumour cells co-evolve with their microenvironment to evade therapy and persist, including tumour dormancy, which is funded by a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship. Methods are statistical modelling, data integration and machine learning applied to bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, plus digital pathology. Current projects include homologous recombination deficiency in breast cancer, radiotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer, and foundation models for multiomics and H&E images.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in cancer genomics, somatic mutation analysis, ML for genomics and single-cell/spatial omics, but the lab does little structural-variant or WGS-focused work, and a UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Bartlett Lab
entries.focus: The group works on statistical genomics and statistics for cell biology. Its main tools are stochastic network models and sparse multivariate models, fitted in frequentist or Bayesian frameworks. Recent work includes a stochastic bipartite-network approach to clustering and visualising single-cell genomic count data (GMM-LE and UMAP-LE, in a Laplacian eigenspace). It also includes gene-regulatory network inference that uses epigenomic priors (iScience, 2026). Earlier work covers fusing single-cell transcriptome and DNA-binding data for network inference in cortical development, and DNA methylation array normalisation.

fit.reason: The group overlaps on computational methods and single-cell omics, but it is methodological and statistical. It does not cover cancer genomics, whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. Visa needs for a UK role also apply.

entries.name: Computational Physics of Chromatin
entries.focus: The group aims to explain the molecular-level mechanisms that control 3D genome organisation at the nanoscale. It builds multiscale computational models of chromatin, anchored in all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, coarse-graining and statistical-mechanical theory. It works with experimental collaborators. A major theme is biomolecular phase separation and liquid-like chromatin organisation, including condensates and how DNA packaging relates to gene regulation. The work is physics-based simulation of chromatin, not sequencing data analysis.

fit.reason: The lab does physics-based molecular simulation of chromatin, with almost no overlap with cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants, ML for genomics or single-cell omics. The only link is a loose one through chromatin and genome organisation, and the UK visa requirement adds friction.

entries.focus: The lab uses single-cell and spatial genomics to build cell atlases of healthy and diseased human tissues. It does this largely through the Human Cell Atlas. A major theme is immunity, including thymus and T cell development, tissue-resident immune cells, and immune development during pregnancy. The group builds computational methods and data portals for single-cell and spatial data, such as batch correction, clustering, scVDJ/TCR analysis and AI models. A smaller cancer-related thread covers anti-cancer immunity in organoids (joint with the Garnett lab) and spatial organisation of glioma (joint with the Saez-Rodriguez lab).

Recent postdoc job postings describe genomics of myeloid disorders, specifically progression from myelodysplastic syndrome to secondary AML.

entries.focus: The group works on human and pathogen statistical genomics, mainly Plasmodium falciparum malaria. entries.focus: The group develops mathematical and computational methods for biological systems, centred on multiscale and stochastic modelling. entries.focus: The group studies how genetic variation shapes immune cell function and contributes to immune-mediated disease. Its work has three parts. Computational work includes statistical genetics, fine-mapping and multi-omic single-cell analysis.

entries.focus: NVIDIA builds BioNeMo, an open-source framework and set of NIM microservices for training and deploying biomolecular AI models at scale on GPUs. entries.name: Amazon / AWS
entries.focus: AWS's life-science work is mostly a platform and partner business. It is not a single research lab. In April 2026 AWS launched Amazon Bio Discovery at its Life Sciences Symposium in New York. It is an agentic AI application for early-stage drug and antibody design, with a catalogue of biological foundation models that users can fine-tune on their own experimental data. Candidates can be sent to partner wet labs, such as Twist Bioscience, and the results feed back into the system. Early adopters include MSK, Bayer, the Broad Institute and Voyager Therapeutics. AWS also provides cloud infrastructure for genomics and omics pipelines to pharma and research institutes. A separate AWS, BCG and Merck platform targets clinical-trial site selection. I found no public Amazon research group on cancer genomics, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

fit.reason: The Bio Discovery work is about antibody and drug design, and I found no Amazon research on cancer genomics, SVs or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is generic ML-for-biology and genomics infrastructure, and the PhD internships I found are general ML roles.

entries.name: Eli Lilly
entries.focus: Lilly launched TuneLab in September 2025. It is an AI/ML platform that gives smaller biotechs access to drug-discovery models trained on more than $1B of Lilly research data. The models cover early discovery decisions, including predictive safety and pharmacokinetics (ADME). They are trained on data from hundreds of thousands of molecules. TuneLab uses federated learning, so partners can use the models without exposing their proprietary data. Partners can contribute data to improve the models, and Lilly plans to add more models, such as in vivo small-molecule predictive models. TuneLab sits within Lilly Catalyze360, Lilly's support suite for early-stage biotechs. The sources I found describe small-molecule drug discovery, not cancer genomics or sequencing-based work. Fuchs's mandate as Chief AI Officer spans drug discovery, clinical trials, manufacturing and commercial work.

fit.reason: Lilly's AI and TuneLab work centres on small-molecule discovery models. It has little visible overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants or single-cell and spatial omics, though the internship lists computational biology and AI/ML as possible project areas.

entries.focus: Recursion is a clinical-stage 'TechBio' company that runs large-scale automated experiments in wet-lab biology and applies machine learning to the results to find drugs.
